title: Do This Every Morning: What calf raises Does to Your Achilles tendon
description: Calf raises with your morning coffee still brewing. The Achilles is the strongest tendon you own, and it answers to a daily signal. Take the calf test, get your number, and see what four weeks of mornings does.

scenes.narration: One leg only. | Heel hanging free. | Rise up slowly. | Full height, every rep. | Down below the step. | Count until you fail. | That count is your NUMBER. | Per leg. Write it down. | Calf raises every morning | is the habit on trial. | What do they do | to your ACHILLES TENDON? | The strongest cable you own. | Week one, it whispers. | Week four, it answers. | At the end | I grade your number.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN SOFT AND SPRINGY
scenes.sub: under 8: untrained - over 25: a real spring
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Fifteen slow single-leg raises is where a soft calf becomes a springy one. Under eight, your Achilles is simply untrained, and it trains beautifully. Over twenty five, you already own a spring most sprinters would respect. Today is the coordinate. The morning habit is about to wind that spring tighter, one sunrise at a time.

Week one whispers. The raises feel easy for three days, almost too easy to matter. Then a deep warmth starts living in your calf, and the stairs at work feel oddly bouncy. That bounce is the tendon taking up the daily signal. The Achilles does not shout like a muscle. It accumulates, quietly, the way interest accumulates. Small deposits, every morning, no days off from the bank.

Week two, the lowering phase becomes the star. You start sinking below the step on purpose, slow as honey, and the tendon lights up along its whole length. Week three, your walk changes. There is a push at the end of every step that was not there before. Week four, retest. Most skinny guys add five to ten strict reps per leg in a month. By week four the morning raises stop being exercise and become inspection. You can feel the difference between a springy day and a flat day through the tendon, the way a driver feels a road through the wheel. That feedback is a skill in itself. Athletes call it listening to the tissue. You built it with a kettle and a step.

Here is the hidden system. The Achilles tendon is a spring rated for tonnes. When you walk, run or jump, it stretches and snaps back, returning energy your muscles would otherwise have to buy. A spring only stays springy if it is used at full stretch, under real load, often. Morning raises do exactly that, and the tendon responds by weaving its collagen tighter, raising its stiffness, and sharpening the snap. The Achilles has one more party trick worth your respect. It is the main spring of your stride, and every step you take all day long cashes the cheque your morning raises wrote. Train the spring for two minutes at sunrise and ten thousand steps spend the improvement for you. No other tendon in your body offers that exchange rate.
Raise with me. Slow up, slower down, heel below the step. Feel the whole cable load. Go.

The protocol: two sets per leg every morning, slow up, three seconds down, heel dropping below the step. Straight knee most days, bent knee once or twice a week for the deeper calf. The mistake is bouncing, which lets momentum steal the tendon's work. The other mistake is skipping the lowering. The way down is where the Achilles earns its stiffness, so own every millimetre of it.

So, your number. Under eight per leg: an untrained spring, and your first month will feel like winding a clock. Eight to fifteen: the spring is waking. Over fifteen: you are wired, and mornings will keep the snap sharp. Retest on day thirty, same step, same slow tempo. Put your number in the comments. Just the number.
Thirty mornings from now your steps will end with a push. Subscribe, and we retest together. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
